svg.title: Urna Aberta: one ballot's continuous path from an offline machine to a blockchain and public checking
svg.desc: A continuous 56-second animation with on-screen captions that change every 8 seconds; one picture keeps moving without slides. You choose, and the offline machine records your vote as an encrypted ballot marked with a green dot. Before you decide, the machine prints receipt R7 with the same green dot and no candidate. Confirm keeps the ballot encrypted. The dashed ballot illustrates testing instead of confirming: it is opened, voided, and you vote again; a test can reveal whether the machine recorded a different choice. Once voting closes, the confirmed ballot joins a signed batch with other ballots, and the batch becomes a new block on a blockchain, under public rules for accepting it. The published ballots are added while still encrypted into one encrypted sum. Three of five trustees contribute key shares to open only that sum, showing an illustrative total without numbers; one share is not enough. An independent verifier takes your receipt, finds your ballot in the published blockchain record and marks it included. Public data and proofs then feed the verifier, which recomputes the total without the voting machine's software. The final view shows the whole path, the two checks, ballot included and total recomputed, and the receipt back in front. R7 is a symbolic code, not a real receipt. Educational prototype on a local blockchain (Anvil); it does not claim absolute secrecy.

g.text: You choose. The machine records your vote.
As in Brazil, you vote offline. The receipt adds a way to check your ballot.
The receipt comes before you confirm or test.
A test can then reveal whether the machine recorded a different choice.
Once voting closes, batches go to the blockchain.
The batches are available for checking, under public rules for accepting them.
The votes are added while still encrypted.
The count can be repeated without revealing each voter’s choice.
Three trustees reveal the total together.
One key share is not enough: opening the sum requires three working together.
Your receipt is checked against the public records.
Brazil’s bulletin shows station totals; this receipt lets you check your ballot’s inclusion.
The data and proofs let you check the count without using the voting machine’s software.
Educational prototype · local blockchain (Anvil) · illustrative total
